'''Michael L. Gross''' (born 1940) is Professor of Chemistry, Medicine, and Immunology, at [[Washington University in St. Louis]] and at [[Washington University School of Medicine]]. He was formerly Professor of Chemistry at [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] from 1968–1994.
He is recognized for his contributions to the field of mass spectrometry and ion chemistry. He is credited with the discovery of [[distonic ion]]s, chemical species containing a radical and an ionic site on different atoms of the same molecule.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L|author2=McLafferty, FW|title=Identification of C3H6+ Structural Isomers by Ion Cyclotron Resonance Spectroscopy|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1971|volume=93|pages=1267–1268|doi=10.1021/ja00734a043|issue=5}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L|title=An Ion Cyclotron Resonance Study of the Structure of C3H6+ and the Mechanism of its Reaction with Ammonia|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1972|volume=94|pages=3744–3748|doi=10.1021/ja00766a013|issue=11}}</ref>

== Career ==
Working with colleagues at the Environmental Protection Agency, he validated the part-per-trillion analysis of 2378-tetrachlorodibenzodioxin in biological tissues, perhaps the first validation of an ultra-trace analytical chemistry method.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=T. Sun |author3=P.A. Lyon |author4=S.F. Wojinski |author5=D.R. Hilker |author6=A.E. Dupuy Jr |author7=R.G. Heath |title=Method Validation Study for Analysis of Tetrachlorodibenzodioxin (TCDD) at the Low Parts-Per-Trillion Level|journal=Analytical Chemistry|year=1981|volume=53|pages=1902–1906|doi=10.1021/ac00235a600|pmid=7294356|issue=12}}</ref> With this method, he and his coworkers found this highly toxic compound in the tissue of veterans of the Vietnam War,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=J.O. Lay Jr |author3=P.A. Lyon |author4=D. Lippstreu |author5=N. Kangas |author6=R.L. Harless |author7=S.E. Taylor |author8=A.E. Dupuy Jr |title=2,3,7,8-Tetrachlorodibenzo-p-dioxin Levels in Adipose Tissue of Vietnam Veterans|journal=Environmental Research|year=1984|volume=33|pages=261–268|doi=10.1016/0013-9351(84)90022-7|pmid=6692811|issue=1|bibcode=1984ER.....33..261G }}</ref> a controversial observation that was later validated by scientists at the Center for Disease Control. <!-- In the early 1980s, he served as chief analytical chemistry witness, Before the Environmental Protection Agency of the United States of America, 2,4,5-T and Silvex Cancellation Hearing, In re: THE DOW CHEMICAL COMPANY, et al. FIFRA Docket Nos. 415. -->

In 1978, he became Director of a National Science Foundation Center for Mass Spectrometry at Nebraska. Under the aegis of the NSF, he commissioned the first commercial triple sector tandem mass spectrometer.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=E.K. Chess |author3=P.A. Lyon |author4=F.W. Crow |author5=S. Evans |author6=H. Tudge|title=Triple Analyzer Mass Spectrometry for High Resolution MS/MS Studies|journal=International Journal of Mass Spectrometry and Ion Physics|year=1982|volume=42|pages=243–254|doi=10.1016/0020-7381(82)80069-7|issue=4|bibcode=1982IJMSI..42..243G }}</ref> With this instrumentation, his coworkers and he sequenced the first unknown peptide using soft ionization and tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS).<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=D. McCrery |author3=F. Crow |author4=K.B. Tomer |author5=M.R. Pope |author6=L.M. Ciuffetti |author7=H.W. Knoche |author8=J.M. Daly |author9=L.D. Dunkle|title=Structure of the Toxin from Helminthsporium Carbonum|journal=Tetrahedron Letters|year=1982|volume=23|issue=51 |pages=5381–5384|doi=10.1016/0040-4039(82)80135-4 }}</ref> They also discovered a new class of fragmentation of gas-phase ions later termed "charge-remote fragmentation."<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=K.B. Tomer |author3=F.W. Crow|title=Location of Double Bond Position in Unsaturated Fatty Acids by Negative Ion MS/MS|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1983|volume=105|pages=5487–5488|doi=10.1021/ja00354a055|issue=16}}</ref> and applied it to a wide variety of compounds including fatty acids, lipids, surfactants, steroids, and peptides. An expanded four-sector version was employed to insert noble gas atoms in C-60 and other fullerenes<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=K.A. Caldwell |author3=D.E. Giblin |author4=C.S. Hsu |author5=D. Cox|title=Endohedral Complexes of Fullerene Radical Cations|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1991|volume=113|pages=8519–8521|doi=10.1021/ja00022a048|issue=22}}</ref> and a second noble gas atom in synthetic fullerenes already containing a noble gas atom.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=D.E. Giblin |author3=M. Saunders |author4=H. Jimenez-Vazquez |author5=R J. Cross|title=Incorporation of Helium into Endohedral Complexes of C60 and C70 Containing Noble-Gas Atoms: A Tandem Mass Specttrometry Study|journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society|year=1997|volume=119|pages=9883–9890|doi=10.1021/ja971104l|issue=41}}</ref>

In the late 1970s, [[Charles Wilkins (chemist)|Charles Wilkins]] and Gross built the second Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometer and were the first to use it for analytical applications. Notable were the demonstrations of GC/MS,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=E.B. Ledford Jr |author3=R.L. White |author4=S. Ghaderi |author5=C.L. Wilkins |title=Coupling of Capillary Gas Chromatography and Fourier Transform Mass Spectrometer|journal=Analytical Chemistry|year=1980|volume=52|pages=2450–2451|doi=10.1021/ac50064a056|issue=14}}</ref> laser desorption,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=D.A. McCrery |author3=E.B. Ledford Jr |title=Laser Desorption Fourier Transform Mass Spectrometry|journal=Analytical Chemistry|year=1982|volume=54|pages=1435–1437|doi=10.1021/ac00245a040|issue=8}}</ref> gas pulsing,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L|author2=T.M. Sack|title=Pulsed Valve Interface For Gas Chromatography/Fourier Transform Mass Spectrometry|journal=Analytical Chemistry|year=1983|volume=55|pages=2419–2421|doi=10.1021/ac00264a049|issue=14}}</ref> multiphoton ionization,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=T.M. Sack |author3=D.A. McCrery|title=Gas Chromatography/Multiphoton Ionization Fourier Transform Mass Spectrometry|journal=Analytical Chemistry|year=1985|volume=57|pages=1290–1295|doi=10.1021/ac00284a027|pmid=4037318|issue=7}}</ref> and the development of calibration law for accurate mass measurement.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L |author2=E.B. Ledford Jr |author3=D.L. Rempel |title=Space Charge Effects in Fourier Transform Mass Spectrometry.II|journal=Analytical Chemistry|year=1984|volume=56|pages=2744–2748|doi=10.1021/ac00278a027|pmid=6524653|issue=14}}</ref> More recently, Don Rempel and he described an electrically compensated FTICR trap to improve mass resolving power.<ref>{{cite journal|last=Gross|first=Michael L|author2=Adam M. Brustkern |author3=Don L. Rempel |title=An Electrically Compensated Trap Designed to Eight Order for FT-ICR Mass Spectrometry|journal=Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry|year=2008|volume=19|pages=1281–1285|doi=10.1016/j.jasms.2008.05.016|pmid=18599306|issue=9|pmc=2597068|bibcode=2008JASMS..19.1281B }}</ref>

Gross currently works on structural proteomics where he uses mass spectrometry in developing and implementing new approaches to protein footprinting, hydrogen/deuterium exchange, crosslinking and native MS. He applies these to problems in biochemistry and biophysics, often in collaboration with other investigators.

==Education, awards, editing==
Gross received his B.A. from [[College of Saint Benedict and Saint John's University|Saint John's University]], Minnesota (1962), and his Ph.D. from the [[University of Minnesota]] (1966). He was a postdoctoral fellow at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] (ER Thornton) and [[Purdue University]] (FW McLafferty). For his research contributions, he received the Field and Franklin Award, American Chemical Society (1999), the Midwest Award, ACS (2002), and the JJ Thomson Medal of the Int'l Foundation for Mass Spectrometry (2006), Fellow of AAAS (2017), Analytical Chemistry Award of the American Chemical Society (2018), and the John Fenn Award of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry (2020). He is co-editor of the [[Encyclopedia of Mass Spectrometry]] and was editor-in-chief of the [[Journal of the American Society for Mass Spectrometry]] since its founding in 1990 through 2015. Prior to that appointment, he served as editor of [[Mass Spectrometry Reviews]].

==Publications==
Gross has authored and coauthored over 700 papers and book chapters. He was recognized as 50 Most Cited Chemists Institute for Scientific Information, 1984-1991.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The World's 50 Most Cited Chemists Ranked by Total Citations, 1984-91|journal=Science Watch|date=May 1992|volume=3|issue=4}}</ref> He was recognized in 2010 as the 356th most cited of living chemists.
